sources.entry: Photofield - Experimental fast photo viewer. MIT Docker/Go

summary.one_liner: Photofield is a self-hosted, non-invasive single-binary photo gallery focused on showing many photos at once with fast zoomable, progressively loaded layouts.
summary.what_it_does: Photofield serves photo folders from the file system as browsable collections through a web interface. Each folder can be shown as an album, and collections can be auto-created from subdirectories. It offers several layouts, including a timeline view, and every view can be zoomed. Layouts load progressively from low-resolution previews up to full-quality photos. The README also describes optional semantic search and tagging (alpha), face detection (alpha) via photofield-ai, and reverse geolocation of places. Thumbnails are cached in SQLite, and indexing and metadata extraction run as separate steps. The original files are never modified, and the file system is treated as the source of truth.
use_cases: timeline view of photos like Google Photos
view photos from a Synology Moments or Photo Station library
read-only photo browsing from mounted folders
how_to_run: mkdir data (empty) in the working directory and put photos in a photos directory
Optionally create configuration.yaml in the data dir to define collections
Binaries: download and unpack a release, then run ./photofield (or photofield.exe)
Optional: install exiftool and djpeg (libjpeg-turbo) for better metadata and JPEG speed
notable: Single static binary with optional dependencies, plus Docker images
Read-only, file-system-based collections that never touch original photos
Progressive multi-resolution loading from low-res previews to full quality
Local embedded reverse geolocation of roughly 50 thousand places
Thumbnails stored in SQLite, reusing Synology Moments / Photo Station thumbnails
caveats: Not optimized for many simultaneous clients; state is kept on the server, so CPU and memory can become a problem
No user accounts, authentication or authorization
Initial layout of a page can be slow with a slow CPU or cold HDD cache; no permalinks that survive database removal or file moves
